The Call
Glory Chai, Rajgarh bus stand. 6:02 AM. Your phone has been ringing for eleven seconds.
Unknown number. Delhi code.
Nobody calls from Delhi at six in the morning with good news.
{first}. Rathore. Sit down if you're standing.
Sunny Bhai turned approver last night. He gave the court everything. Including the fact that you never fixed a single ball.
The Board reviewed your case at midnight. The ban is lifted. Effective today.
Two years of washing glasses. Two years of people crossing the road when they saw me.
Don't thank me. Thank whoever made him so scared he started talking. And {first}? Answer your phone today. All day.
Six months. Five hundred and forty glasses of chai a day. Not one ball bowled at you.
The suspension ended at midnight. I stayed up to watch the clock change.
Another call. A different Delhi number.
Good morning. National selection office. Is this {first}?
You've been named in the thirty probables for the national camp. Report to the National Academy, Bengaluru. Monday, 7 AM.
Congratulations. Please don't post about it until the Board announces it.
The line goes dead. The kettle is boiling over. You don't move.
Kya hua? Who died?
Thirty probables. Fifteen make the squad. Eleven play. One cap.
"Papa. National camp. Bengaluru."
Tell him first. He earned it.
Call Pandey-ji before anyone.
He saw it before anyone did.
Call Neha.
She'll want the scoop.
Bengaluru.
He sets the kettle down very carefully, like it might break. Then he walks out to the bus stand and tells the 6:15 to Meerut. Every passenger.
My son! National camp! Free chai for everyone today. Except you, Sharma-ji, you still owe me from Diwali.
...I know. Kabir called me last night to ask if you can handle short balls.
I told him you learned on a tyre. He laughed. Make him stop laughing, beta.
It's 6 AM. This better be big.
WAIT.
National camp??? I'm writing it. I'm writing it NOW.
...Proud of you, cricketer.
You never call before 9.
Oh my God. OH MY GOD.
Delhi to Bengaluru is a two-hour flight. Just saying.
I'm crying in a newsroom. Thanks a lot.
By 9 AM the whole bus stand knows. By 10, the local news van is parked where the old stall burned down.
Three tiffins. Aloo, paneer, and one with ghee rotis that you will NOT share with anyone.
Bhaiya, if you meet Karan Dhillon you HAVE to get me a selfie. He's the captain. He's perfect. He has dimples.
He is a married man, Pinky.
I said dimples, Maa, not marriage.
Saw the list.
Enjoy Bengaluru, chaiwala. Some of us were born for this.
Two years and he still can't spell my name. Fine. I'll make him say it.
Saw the list. Room 214, they put us next door.
Don't snore. And don't get dropped before me, it'll look bad for both of us.
Late. The stall is shut. You're counting the day's money when a black car with tinted windows stops at the bus stand. It doesn't belong in Rajgarh.
A man in a grey suit steps out and holds out an envelope. Thick cream paper. No name on it.
Take the envelope.
Curiosity.
"Whoever sent you, I'm not interested."
You've been here before.
Inside: a platinum card, embossed with one name. RAGHAV MEHRA. On the back, in fountain pen: "Welcome to the big leagues."
And a photograph. You. A hotel lobby. Two years ago. Shaking hands with Sunny Bhai.
The man doesn't argue. He places the envelope on your counter, on top of the day's coins, and drives away.
It falls open. A photograph. You, two years ago, in a hotel lobby, shaking hands with Sunny Bhai.
Someone kept the photo for two years. Someone waited for you to matter.
